stem: When assessing long-term outcomes for intestinal transplant recipients beyond six months, which finding is reported in standard outcome references?

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition has been discontinued in a majority of recipients
Every recipient remains TPN-dependent indefinitely in all reported cohorts
Intestinal transplant recipients never return to normal activities
Graft survival is unaffected by recipient age in all studies

explanation.rationale_correct: Long-term intestinal transplant outcome data report that most recipients are well or have only minor issues after six months, and TPN has been discontinued in a majority of recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Outcome references report TPN discontinuation in 67% of recipients, not universal lifelong TPN dependence.
rationale_incorrect.C: Most recipients have returned to normal activities at greater than six months post-transplant.
rationale_incorrect.D: Improved graft survival is associated with younger recipient age among reported outcome factors.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: TPN has been discontinued in 67% of recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 13 → intestinal transplant outcomes (>6 months: activities, TPN discontinuation); PDF p. 681 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. First intestine organ tag in bank; anchor verified on Cupples p. 681.

stem: A kidney recipient living three hours from the transplant center has stable graft function and follows with a community nephrologist. According to long-term management references, what coordination expectation applies?

options.text: There should be frequent and open communication between community physicians and the transplantation center
The transplant center should cease involvement once a community nephrologist is identified
Community physicians should manage immunosuppression changes without ever contacting the transplant team
Follow-up may occur only at the transplant center and never with community providers

explanation.rationale_correct: Long-term follow-up may occur with the transplant center or experienced community physicians, but frequent open communication between community providers and the transplantation center is expected.

rationale_incorrect.B: The transplant center should remain a source of care and expertise even when community follow-up occurs.
rationale_incorrect.C: Immunosuppression changes require coordinated communication with the transplant center.
rationale_incorrect.D: References explicitly allow follow-up with community nephrologists or internists experienced in transplant care.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 11, Post-transplant Long-term Management → follow-up setting and communication paragraph
primary_anchor.quote_hint: There should be frequent and open communication between the community physicians and the transplantation center

references.locator: Ch. 11 → follow-up with community nephrologist/internist and center communication; PDF p. 302 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Distinct 030500 angle from cctc-3007 (visit frequency); anchor verified on Danovitch p. 302.

stem: During discharge medication teaching for a kidney recipient starting tacrolimus, which instruction is MOST important to emphasize about dosing schedule?

options.text: Take critical-dose immunosuppressants at the same time every day for therapeutic drug monitoring
Take tacrolimus at different random times each day to improve absorption
Skip trough-level blood draws on the day doses are taken on schedule
Double the dose automatically after any single late dose without team contact

explanation.rationale_correct: Discharge teaching stresses taking medications at the same time every day; critical-dose drugs such as tacrolimus must be taken at specific intervals to allow therapeutic drug monitoring, especially on blood-draw days.

rationale_incorrect.B: Inconsistent dosing times undermine trough monitoring and are not appropriate teaching.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recipients must understand dosing timing relative to scheduled trough levels.
rationale_incorrect.D: Dose adjustments require transplant team guidance rather than automatic doubling.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → medication education → Right time
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Taking medications at the same time every day is very important

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → medication education → Right time (critical-dose drugs and trough timing); PDF p. 107 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Distinct 030600 angle from cctc-3008 (missed dose/vomiting); anchor verified on Cupples p. 107.

stem: A simultaneous pancreas-kidney recipient two weeks post-transplant has rising creatinine and decreased urine amylase from a bladder-drained pancreas graft. Evaluate the following statements about pancreas allograft monitoring:

elements.text: In SPK transplantation, elevated serum creatinine can serve as a surrogate marker of pancreas rejection.
Decreased urine amylase may occur with pancreas graft rejection when the graft is bladder drained.
Hyperglycemia is an early sign of pancreas transplant rejection.
Glucose levels may remain normal in the initial stages of pancreas rejection.

explanation.rationale_correct: SPK recipients share immunologic risk, so rising creatinine may reflect pancreas rejection; decreased urine amylase can signal rejection in bladder-drained grafts. Hyperglycemia is a later sign, while glucose may remain normal early in rejection.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—glucose can remain normal early in pancreas rejection.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; hyperglycemia is not an early rejection sign.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 15, Pancreas Transplantation → acute rejection monitoring (SPK creatinine, urine amylase, hyperglycemia timing)
primary_anchor.quote_hint: elevated serum creatinine levels can serve as a surrogate marker of pancreas rejection … Hyperglycemia: Not an early sign

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 15 → acute pancreas rejection monitoring (statements I–II, IV; negation of III); PDF p. 847 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. First kidney_pancreas organ tag; third complex_combo in bank; anchor verified on Cupples p. 847.
